TABLING OF TEXTS OF INSTRUMENTS ADOPTED
speechtext:
I wish to table the bilingual texts of the instruments adopted at the 46th session of the international labour conference held in Geneva, Switzerland, in June 1962.
The Canadian delegation, consisting of government, employer and worker representatives, was headed by the deputy minister of labour. The conference debated at some length the report of the director general of the I.L.C. which was centred on this occasion mainly on the subject of older people in work and retirement. Among numerous resolutions, one was proposed by Canada. This dealt with measures to strengthen research in the labour field both nationally and internationally, and was adopted unanimously by the conference.
The four instruments tabled herewith are convention 117 on basic aims and standards of social policy; convention 118 on equality of treatment of nationals and non-nationals in the field of social security; recommendation 116 on reduction of hours of work, and recommendation 117 on vocational training.
An attached letter of October 24, 1962, states that the Minister of Justice is of the opinion that the subject matter of each of these instruments is partially within federal legislative jurisdiction and partially within provincial legislative jurisdiction. According to the usual procedure I am asking my colleague the Secretary of State to send a set of these instruments, together with the justice opinion, to the lieutenant governor of each province, with the request that they be placed before the competent legislative authority in the province for consideration. At the federal level, the Department of Labour will study the subject matter of each instrument in consultation with other departments concerned and will consider what further steps are feasible in this connection.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, at the evening adjournment last night I had mentioned the importance-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext: Order. I think it would be helpful to the hon. member if those members who wish to leave the chamber would do so expeditiously and quietly so that he can complete his remarks.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last evening I was suggesting that one of the important services of the national economic development board would be to assist Canada to find its way into an integration with its Atlantic allies under the ideas suggested in the second clause of the NATO treaty. This was something very important to my leader. It is something that was very important to Jean Monnet, architect of the common market, who feels that there is nothing more important now than the movement toward an


Atlantic community in which common institutions will be increasingly developed to meet any problems. Jean Monnet praises Britain joining the general movement toward a united Europe, something that even as we debate this matter today is in the shadow of doubt, perhaps, but nevertheless great things are happening in respect of Britain that we cannot fail to recognize.
Mr. Speaker, may I read one short paragraph from Jean Monnet's article published in The Rotarian of October, 1961. He says:
That we have begun to co-operate on these affairs at the Atlantic level is a great step forward. It is evident that we must soon go a good deal further toward an Atlantic community.
The creation of a united Europe brings this nearer by making it possible for America and Europe to act as partners on an equal footing.
The reason is not only to maximize the wealth of this Atlantic community itself. It is actually the preservation of the peace of all, and second to assure the generous contribution of this vitally important group of nations to the development of the underdeveloped countries. We find in Canada in this past year that an outstanding businessman such as William E. Williams, president of Procter & Gamble of Canada, recommends an economic union between Canada and the United States. Douglas W. Ambridge, president of Abitibi Power & Paper Co. Ltd., recommends a North American market involving Canada, the United States and Mexico, to serve as something of a magnet for the Latin American countries. Why? Because this is a clear step in the direction we must take toward forming some larger Atlantic integration.
We on this side of the house would have been very happy to have done this more directly with integration with Britain when the opportunity presented itself some years ago, but that opportunity was not seized and there must be other ways in which this great plan may still be realized.
We may ask is it possible to do such a thing with the United States. I will read to the house the words of President Kennedy in his July 4 message at Philadelphia. This time the president was not talking about George Washington or anything of that sort. He said:
I will say, here and now, on this day of Independence, that the United States will be ready for a declaration of interdependence-that we will be prepared to discuss with a united Europe the ways and means of forming a concrete Atlantic partnership.
It is not sufficient for the Prime Minister of Canada to nurse his wrath and prepare to gird his loins for a new campaign against the United States, against Britain or against anybody else. Surely our policy must be one of planning toward this larger world order

-but time is running out. While other countries have been moving ahead Canada has been standing still. We cannot afford to let another year go by without taking decisive action.

Surely what we in Canada are really striving for is a bold new economic consensus. We know that in the past we have had important royal commissions. We have had the Rowell-Sirois and the Gordon commissions with penetrating substantive studies of the Canadian economy which proved of great importance in solving some of the problems we have already faced. It is unfortunate that many of the recommendations of the Gordon commission were not implemented, and to some extent have been thwarted and frustrated in the past several years.
In any event we feel-and this was one of the many recommendations of the Gordon commission-that there must be a continuing study of economic. problems based on long range considerations. We heard engaging speeches last evening from the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, who took us on a tour of the north, and an address from the Associate Minister of National Defence on the glory of France and the glory of this administration. The first new problem is the fact that in the four years from 1958 to 1961 Canada averaged over 6i per cent of unemployment. Actually according to a minister of the Ontario government, Hon. Robert Macaulay last year, it was over 6 per cent. So we have, according to that authority at least, five years of over 6 per cent unemployment 27507-3-189
in Canada. In 1960 we had the most shockingly large figure of unemployment of any industrial country in the world.

We had the prognostications of the Gordon commission to study with regard to where we should have been this past year. We should have been far ahead. The final important point, Mr. Speaker, is the question of balance of payments. I submit that the questions of unemployment, growth and productivity are new problems with which this administration has failed to deal, but they inherited in part a problem that we knew something about, the problem of balance of payments. This calls for the most earnest consideration of long term principles. In this matter of the balance of payments I want to tell the house that in the last six years our obligations in respect of the goods and services we have bought from foreigners have exceeded by $6 billion the obligations owing to us for the goods and services we have sold to foreigners. We have settled these deficits by selling off our Canadian resources and Canadian owned companies and going into debt. I am quoting the words of a distinguished author, the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon). Bruce Hutchison asserts that we are alienating our heritage to the point where we are in jeopardy in Canada of actually losing our economic and political independence.
We do not believe for one moment that with the establishment of a national economic development board a cabinet can sit down and simply be told what to do. There is something that goes with this. Policy has to be provided, and policy has to be provided very shortly, by an administration that is able to face facts, study situations and take action, courageous action, and not just look the other way when difficult problems present themselves. I think that with the combination of the establishment of this kind of integrating board and a bold and courageous administration, one that is looking ahead to the long run and not just to the next general election, Canada could have a glorious economic future.

Mr. Speaker, during the time available to me today I want to make three points. The first is that planning on a national scale is a necessity. The second is that such planning should be carried out essentially in human and not in monetary terms. The third is that effective co-operation between management and labour in this country will only come about if we have inspired leadership from government. This is evident to all.
As far as planning is concerned, I believe we have no choice because the business of government has become far too cumbersome, far too all embracing. Fifteen per cent or one in seven at least of the people employed in this country are working in the civil service. Roughly one third of our income is taken away from us in taxes. Government, by taxing us and influencing us in this way, is undoubtedly having a great deal to say about how we work and whether or not we prosper.
Government obviously then must be interested in looking ahead and planning intelligently. But it must do more than plan intelligently. It must also inspire industry, management and labour in this country. It can inspire them in various ways but one of the most effective ways, I contend, is to prepare competent forecasts of what is likely to happen assuming no change in present policies. If the results compared with the forecasts do not measure up to our fond hopes, then new targets must be established and these targets must be broken down so that they are understandable to industry and so that our various industries can themselves plan more intelligently.
In other words, it is a problem of communication. The government should not only know where it is going but should indicate where it would prefer to go and let industry, management and labour, working together bring about the desired results.
I have used the word "planning" throughout my comments so far. I believe in planning. We all believe in planning. We all believe in looking ahead and attempting to correct trends which we do not like and avoid results which are undesirable to us. But planning in my view, and this is important, comes second to freedom, particularly freedom of the individual. Plans, particularly specific plans laid down by government, must give way where they impinge on the freedom of the individual, the freedom of groups of individuals to go their own way and make their own livelihood as they see fit.
This planning must certainly be adapted to Canadian institutions. In my view planning
National Economic Development Board. at the top government level should be carried out by ministers of the crown. So far as economic affairs are concerned, I believe there should always be a continuing committee of the cabinet on economic affairs. I also believe that this cabinet committee should not be dominated by, or consist solely of, the Minister of Finance. If there is anything in the Social Credit philosophy in which I concur it is that money is essentially a tool. Our monetary affairs must be managed so as to make effective our plans for a better life, greater production and more jobs.
To me the Minister of Finance personifies the man who has control of money. He is holding the reins, and often he is putting on the brake. Certainly he is not the man in the cabinet to put the case for growth. He is not the man in the cabinet to put the case for humanity in the sense of more jobs. In this respect I am more impressed by the arrangements in the United Kingdom. The national economic development board, or "Neddy" as they refer to it in the United Kingdom, has on it not simply the minister of finance but Mr. Industry, the secretary of the board of trade, and also the minister of labour.

We had this situation in the late 1940's and the 1950's in this country. We had a minister of industry and a minister of labour as well as a minister of finance who took an interest in over-all economic growth and planning. As evidence of this planning we had such activities as the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects and its preparation of long term forecasts. We also had cooperation with industry. Evidence of that is to be found in the quarterly meetings of ministers, top level civil servants and business economists the latter representing the views of the various industries and of labour across the country. In other words there was machinery, admittedly voluntary, which resulted in an exchange of views and the trans-

What has happened since? The individuals concerned in those matters have largely been dispersed from Ottawa. Their advice is no longer available, with the result that these channels have largely dried up. I believe we should revive some such arrangement. I also think that this legislation, although admittedly a first step toward a national economic development board, should help us bridge this gap.
I believe there should be a secretariat to this cabinet committee on economic affairs. I believe its chairman should in effect have similar duties to those of the chairman of the proposed national economic development board. He should have around him a board of advisers. He should have under him a substantial staff, and this staff should be preparing long term economic forecasts.
In addition to that, having received instructions from the elected representatives or from the cabinet in respect of desirable targets, courses of action should be taken in respect of improving employment opportunities, correcting our adverse balance of trade with the United States, and so on.
I believe that some of the members of this staff should be acting as rapporteurs. They should act as secretaries for industry committees, committees substantially set up by the industries concerned. These committees should be composed of representatives of both management and labour. These rapporteurs, together with the representatives of industry and labour, will have their eyes lifted from the continuation of the relatively mundane activities of business to improving our national production, also by focusing their eyes on a common objective, that of improving our economy, they will thus be less inclined to quarrel about their differences; less inclined to argue between themselves in respect to wages, profits and so on.
I believe we have had at least one example of this type of thing in recent years. We had, first of all, the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects. Then as a result of the Borden commission a good deal of information was made available to government and to industry in terms of forecasts, particularly in respect of oil. The purchase
[Mr. Davis.l

of oil from outside our border has been one of the major causes of our imbalance of payments. We need to purchase more oil at home for our own consumption, and export more. This royal commission provided this sort of information. It provided a background against which the oil industry was able to do more effective planning. The government of the day took this information seriously and indicated to the oil industry what targets were desirable with regard to our international trade.
These targets, as I understand it, are in large part being met. This is a practical example of "indicative" planning, as the French call it, indicating targets to industry. After the target is indicated the industry bends its efforts toward achieving the target which is substantially in the national interest. If the targets are not met, other methods might have to be instituted by the government to ensure that such problems as the balance of payments are overcome.
Then there are the area boards. We now have an Atlantic development board. The area boards would learn a great deal from the deliberations of these various industry committees. I would envisage two or three dozen such committees publishing reports from time to time as to the prospects of particular industries and as to the changes which might be expected. The area boards could read these reports and understand what, conceivably, could happen with regard to a particular region of the country, what the possibilities were of a decline, an increase and so on, and when they were likely to occur. This would assist in the selection of alternatives for depressed areas, particularly areas of high unemployment.
We have, of course, in this business of planning, particularly in the execution of an effective plan, some rather difficult decisions to make. We cannot simply make forecasts. We cannot rely entirely on the prosperous, growing industries to co-operate, and then go along subsidizing or otherwise supporting the industries and areas which are in difficulties. The field of energy in this country represents roughly 10 per cent of our economy. We have industries which are growing in this field and industries which are declining. The oil and gas industries are expanding, and so is the production of hydro power. All the forecasts, however, indicate that over the next five or ten years the production and consumption of coal is likely to decline. Our governments, both national and provincial, say nothing or do not indicate otherwise. Certainly the policies they follow do not face up to the fact that not only are the requirements for coal declining but that the coal industry is not likely to make its way in competition with

other forms of energy and therefore the number of people employed will be diminishing in ten years' time to about half or 40 per cent of those now employed.
These are the probabilities, these are the trends which our national economic development board, supported by an able secretariat, would have to report. Certainly these are the trends which would be revealed by an effective board reporting publicly and effectively at least once a year.
In so far as energy is concerned at the present time, we have at least four separate departments concerned with that subject. We have the Department of Trade and Commerce concerned with oil and gas. We have the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys concerned with coal and the powers of the dominion coal board. We have the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources concerned with hydro. We have, believe it or not, the Department of Veterans Affairs concerned with atomic energy. In my opinion none of these departments is represented effectively in the deliberations of this proposed national economic development board.
I think we should focus not only on the declining industries such as coal but on the future prospects of industries such as atomic energy. We have been spending currently about $20 million a year on coal subsidies of one kind and another. We are spending roughly $30 million a year on atomic energy. We have already put enough money into atomic energy in this country to build an oil pipe line from Edmonton to Montreal. In other words Montreal, in terms of economics, could be right next to the oil fields of Alberta.
We have decided more or less willy-nilly to go on pumping these tens of millions of dollars into atomic energy. Atomic energy is, perhaps, good for some parts of the country, but is essentially competitive with the resources of Quebec, British Columbia and other parts of the country which still have large untapped reserves of hydroelectric power. A national economic development board would certainly indicate that other priorities might be established in respect of subsidies and assistance for the energy industries. They would urge that by some means of adjustment we arrange that the emphasis be upon industries which are in the economic interest of the country rather than upon the ones which are either outmoded or may not be needed for some considerable time.
There are many other decisions which are difficult and which have to be made by the government, a government learning from the projections and deliberations of the national economic development board. The declining industries would be making people available who would have to be retrained for other 27507-3-190
National Economic Development Board jobs. Certainly the recent legislation with regard to industrial change and manpower adjustment is desirable in this connection. It can provide some machinery, but we should know in advance where these people are likely to be in surplus supply, what new skills are needed and how the people should be retrained. Only by looking ahead, revising our targets and establishing new targets, can we properly provide the direction and encouragement for those who are unemployed and those likely to need training as a result of great improvements in efficiency and productivity.
We have, in another area, the perennial argument between management and labour in respect of annual increases in wages, and so on. Managers, particularly managers concerned with finding export markets, will say, "Our productivity is only improving at the rate of 2 or 3 per cent a year. We cannot afford to pay more or we will be pricing ourselves out of world markets". Labour is inclined to be suspicious of this claim. But if we had an effective national economic development board complete with a capable secretariat, it would be giving industry and labour an indication year by year of the over-all upward trend in productivity gains. It would provide an order of magnitude of wage increases as a result of these improvements in productivity in the whole economy. Labour could certainly be pitching its demands more realistically in terms of wage increases, and management would have a better idea of where it was going, not only in respect of its domestic business but also its competitive position overseas.
Again, Mr. Speaker, with regard to scientific and industrial research, we do not do enough in this country. We should do more. Even with an increase in this type of expenditure we need to know where the emphasis should lie. In this connection government is certainly making the major outlay in this country. It should be placing those moneys into what in the future will be the growth industries, and not running counter to the mainstream of economic development throughout the world. One thing that alarms me very much in this mixed economy of ours, in which much of our income is generated by private enterprise, is that we tax private enterprise. On the other hand we participate, in the form of crown agencies and other government devices, in industries which we, by definition, say that private enterprise is unwilling, perhaps incapable, of carrying out. As a result we often find the greater part of government outlays going into industries which are declining, or certainly less efficient, and tend to restrict the more economic activities, those carried out by private enterprise, through taxation. This
2994	HOUSE OF
National Economic Development Board is certainly a mixed up concept of how to progress and how to make our country more productive.
A national economic development board that was really doing its job would indicate where the real growth prospects are, where the great improvements in efficiency were possible. It would indicate to the government that while subsidies may be necessary in some industry or in some area for a period of time, these should be tapered off and eventually terminated. In this way we would not continually be getting deeper and deeper into the morass, making ourselves less efficient in ever widening areas of our economy.
There are various attitudes to planning. The attitude, generally speaking, of management is favourable. Most people would expect that the formation of a national economic development board would cause a good deal of opposition in business. But business at the management level is accustomed to planning. In our preponderantly free enterprise system we have a great deal of collaboration now in respect of planning. Through the industrial associations, for example, the results of forecasts and plans are published. Even cost data is now made available to competitors in substantial areas of competition. Industry, in the sense of management, is prepared to do this sort of planning and looks to government, and relies upon government and hopes that government will be more predictable on this front.
We see, in the case of France, for example, that management of industry largely took the initiative in the formulation of the national plan for industry in that country. Labour, on the other hand, at least through the voices of their more socialistic representatives, has tended to oppose plans through the management route. Labour in the United Kingdom, for example, has not been very enthusiastic about the establishment of the national economic development board in that country. It saw sinister implications; it saw management in some fashion directing, in perhaps collaboration with the government, more rather than less of the nation's economic affairs. Certainly the trade unions in the United Kingdom have been very suspicious of the formation more recently of yet another board, nicknamed "Nicky", the board which has to do with the establishment of a national incomes policy in the United Kingdom. The hope there is that by preparing general economic data a better measure of what labour and industry might reasonably expect, in terms of wage increases and profits, would be available. The unions have tended to be very cool to this particular board and its purposes.


I trust that in this country we can have better communication between government, management and labour in these respects and that labour will begin to look upon an effective national economic development board as its opportunity for a voice, not only in respect of direction, but accomplishment of the national targets which a far seeing board would set up for us.
Government, I believe, sets the stage. It needs a competent secretariat to give it a feel as to the current, long term trends. I believe our elected representatives should substantially say what is desirable and what is not desirable in the main, and in the broadest context should indicate what targets should be achieved. I believe that in this way government itself could be consistent in respect of its own investment policies; it could be more consistent in respect of tax policies in times of slump and in times of boom. I believe that industry, with management and labour working together and with this over-all information and instruction, can, industry by industry, plan more effectively its own future. Certainly it could be more productive.

I believe that in this way we could have greater output, greater productivity, and this in turn would make possible higher incomes in this country. The consequence of higher incomes certainly could be broader welfare provisions without an increase in taxes. This is very desirable. It is the type of thing for which certainly the Liberal party is striving. It faces head on the problem of providing greater and more extended services to the public, and at the same time not increasing taxation and blunting the initiative of our people. This is very desirable and I believe it is possible with the proper type of democratic planning.
I want to return to the main points which I outlined at the beginning, Mr. Speaker. I believe that we need in this country a sense of national purpose. I believe that every one should be participating, government, management and labour, in this great program. I believe that to operate effectively a national economic development board co-operating with industry and with individual industry's boards set up voluntarily, working to indicated targets, can bring this about. We must take this board seriously. It is not ideal, but I think that in time it could perform a valuable function. I believe it could make use of,

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION OF DUTIES, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
In any
discussion of Canada's future economic development a number of Canadians will spend a great deal of time talking about how they pioneered this continent-and then they drop the discussion. I am not suggesting we should forget about those pioneer days, but what concerns us now is the present. I say "the present" because we can hardly think of the future until we have caught up with the present. The present represents the circumstances we have to face as far as our export products are concerned.
The first thing we have to do in this country is to acknowledge that we are now taking hesitant steps in a direction which has already been pioneered in Europe and in other countries. We have to consider economic development as the opportunity of this age. In other ages opportunities lay with war, exploration, scientific discoveries and inventions. But there is a different opportunity open to us in this country today and that is the opportunity of economic development. We must, therefore, get rid of the economic superstitions and illusions we have been cherishing and realize that we can no longer exist in this hard shell we have placed around our borders. We must realize that though we were prosperous once we now have to take drastic steps to find a place in this new economic era.
During the last war, Europe underwent almost total destruction. Today it has become the co-leader of the productive world. We in Canada have an opportunity of moving into this new age without suffering the type of disruption which Europe had to endure. We do not possess the advanced industrial development of some other countries and we are, therefore, in a position to change our course more easily. It is most important that we in this country should take this big jump- a leap which will shatter all the ideas of outworn economic theories. We do not have as many men with the skill and knowledge necessary for this development and accordingly 27507-3-190J
we must train such people. This can be done as a result of assistance by our government. The western nations have shown us how, with economic assistance in investment and as a result, they have been able to rehabilitate their economies.
Under the terms of the bill we are now discussing the chairman of the proposed board can be appointed for a period of office of ten years. His responsibilities are set out, along with the duties of the board, in one of the subsections. This chairman could become the second most powerful man in our country. I would suggest to the government that he should report to a group of ministers in the cabinet, namely a new minister of industry, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Labour, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The chairman should become part of this committee. In my experience, and in the experience of others, it is more efficient to have a chairman of a board of this type report to a select group of people so that those people may take the action which is necessary.
The national economic development board, if it is not to be just a phrase, must become the centre of our whole economic theory for this country. This is what the Japanese did after the last war and, as a result, they have become extremely successful. In short, with this national economic development board we are embarking on a new way of life, and the Canadian people, if they endorse this idea, must put everything they have into it. I say we must have Canada moving into gear. Let us not waste any more time than we have already wasted. The day of gradual growth is over. There are acquisitions and amalgamations. I suggest it is one of the great responsibilities of this board to set a standard for the yearly increase of productivity in this country. I think our first prime minister, Sir John A. Macdonald, had an outstanding idea in his national policy for economic development. None of us here anticipate a long life for this government and, therefore, it would prove an advantage if, in these days of minority government, we could get together as a parliament and adopt a Canadian policy. The co-operation of management and workers of which I have spoken comes about only as a result of prodding by the government. The new responsibility of government, of management and of the workers is the responsibility to work together for the national good, which, in the final sense, is the good of the individual.
All hon. members have, I am sure, read the report to the national productivity council of the mission to Europe. This is, in my opinion, the most outstanding achievement of this
2996	HOUSE OF COMMONS
National Economic Development Board
council. The report made one important thing clear. While labour management and government co-operation was not the factor wholly responsible for Europe's economic resurgence, nevertheless co-operation was the core of this whole development. There were, of course, other important factors. We all know of the heavy investment of United States capital in those countries, of the new plants which were built and the new equipment which was installed. Moreover, in those countries wage scales were lower than in the United States. This was a vital factor because a wage incentive remained-there was always the possibility of more pay being given for more work. On the part of ownership and management there was appreciation of the fact that profits could not be unrestricted. Of course, no economic system can develop without profit because profit is needed for reinvestment. But no management or employer can operate a business at abnormal profits while asking labour to produce more for less or for the same reward. As I have already stated, we have to do this in order to compete in world markets, which means that we have to price our products on a world competitive basis. I am not suggesting that everything that Europe has done is right, but I am suggesting that we must compete with these people, and if we are to compete with them, we must compete with them on the same basis. In this country not only must we go into the second half of this century with a responsible and modern government-management-worker co-operation and with new export ideas; we also have to do other things. This means quite simply that we have to supply our own people with the tools to compete on world markets, and these tools are the languages, the customs and the real needs of our potential customers.
What have we really done along this line? The government's productivity council in my opinion was poorly conceived, and so poorly conceived that in its first year it lost its main managerial representative and its main organized labour representative. I do not think it is necessary to describe the work of the labour-management council because we are all familiar with it, but it is constructive to note how the British system works and how it could be applied to Canada. It is also interesting and important to understand the industry-wide bargaining between labour and management which is the case in Europe. What I should particularly like to point out is that in the European countries, or in a large bulk of them, management is organized much the same as labour is organized, thus , creating a balance of power in which the government sits in the centre and acts as

a referee. What we have to do in the national economic development board, and also what the government has to do in the national economic development board, is to get public opinion behind it. I think we all recognize and understand how very important this is.
Can we compare today the first 62 days of this session with the first 100 days of President Roosevelt's term of office in 1933?
I have a note here which says:
On Thursday, March 16, 1933, less than two weeks after his inauguration, Roosevelt asked the congress for a new federal concept for the American farmer-national planning for U.S. agriculture.
That was in 1933. This country and this government, if this idea is to work, have to do something dramatic, such as that which happened in Ontario with Sir Adam Beck and the hydro, or as Roosevelt did with TVA, or as the Egyptians have recently done with the Aswan dam, or as we Canadians did when the St. Lawrence seaway was conceived and placed into operation, when we decided that if the American people would not cooperate with us in this great project we would go it alone. I believe that we have to understand planning in its valuable, modern, capitalistic and free enterprise sense. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) said in the last election, as quoted in the Globe and Mail of October 25, 1961, that "the issue in the next election would be free enterprise versus socialism". I think we all realize now that this was not the issue in the last election and I doubt very much that it will be the issue in the next election.
It could be that a lack of any planning at the top is at the bottom of our economic troubles today. The essential factor in planning of this type is that it should not be put solely into administrative agencies, which are uncontrollable by their nature, but that the agencies work and be controlled within the framework of the parliamentary system. Governments can be put out of office, which is why any system of planning must be controlled by the elected representatives of government who can protect the national good. Economic planning boards or productivity councils appointed by the government should be presided over by a permanent secretary, but come within the jurisdiction of a national economic development council chaired by a minister of the crown, with other ministers as members and with representatives from industrial management, agriculture, trade unions and universities. What has to be done now in what eminent economists call the "break-through moment" is this. No longer can we look for gradual improvements. This

is a "take-off crisis", and there must be a leap in getting off the ground, which is the most difficult phase of planning. The initial leap has to be pushed and pursued, and it will be quite a time before it can, as in the European common market countries feed on itself. There can be no new economic development until at least one tenth of the national income over and above the investment needed to maintain a growing population at the same standard of living is put into productive investment.
We should also remember and should understand that industrial productivity for export and international trade is not our only consideration. There is a great deal of work yet to be done in this country in community services, such as highways, transport, communications, distribution and credit. We can learn one very valuable lesson. During the building of our railways in this country there was provided a major economic impetus to the economy. We used our Canadian talents and materials to this end, and we have by no means yet completed our transportation and communications systems across the country. We are now also up against the growing problems of extra people moving into urban areas because of higher and greater efficiency in farming areas. This is going to mean that these people must be retrained for more productive jobs. As we are preparing for a major economic change in development, we are going to be caught for a long time in a dilemma between not spending enough on our foundation programs, starving our economic development and conjuring up inflation by putting investment into unproductive, though sometimes popular, channels.
What I am going to say now does not make for political popularity, but it must be said in the interests of genuine and stable permanent development. We need jobs in this country and we need them very badly; but there is the danger of confusing the creation of jobs with economic growth. Uneconomic investment made to create what can be only temporary jobs depletes the country's resources. Unemployment is a danger certainly, and it is a terrible problem; but stagnation is more dangerous since it produces more unemployment.
I would therefore suggest that our economic planning must consider the direction of investment as well as the finding of capital. I would also suggest that our N.H.A. loans available to people in order to build homes should also be available to people in order to build factories, and in cutting the rate of unemployment which is recommended by this board, for the producing of products that
National Economic Development Board can be sold competitively outside our country. We need capital and we need external capital. Europe and the Marshall plan is an excellent example. We must remember that we must not sell off all of our natural assets in order to acquire this capital. Most rate impetus in an economy is based upon the influx of foreign capital but this must be controlled, and it certainly was controlled in the case of the United States.
I should now like to discuss some countries such as Holland and Belgium. These are useful examples, I believe. Even as the minister pointed out, in creating this national economic development board we must remember our own particular problems. It is interesting to note that a small country such as Holland exports 50 per cent of its products and the great emphasis that is placed in that country upon a lower wage scale. However, this is accompanied by full employment. Wages in that country are increased only on the basis of productivity. However, they are only increased with the proviso that by increasing wages and prices they do not place themselves outside the pricing of world competition. There is a strong sense of friendship between labour, management and government in that country.
There is also the interesting case of Poland with respect to the production of agricultural products. These people have the ability and the land with which to produce wheat but instead of producing wheat in sufficient volume to feed their country, they import it. Poland has found it can produce more productive products which can be sold and which are more valuable to them, than is the production of wheat for their own consumption. This is the kind of thing that I suggest we in Canada must do. What can we produce for ourselves and what is most profitable to the Canadian people?
I suggest that we must take this leap into modem economic development in Canada. We must provide the leadership for voluntary cooperation for mutual improvement. We must employ new concepts for labour management relations with the government as a partner- and I am sure that all of us have the government as a partner-and I suggest as a partner and not as a big brother. We in this chamber have the responsibility of guiding and controlling the total destinies of capital, management and labour. We must abandon any isolationist ideas and understand that today we are part of a large international community. Most of all, we must have in this country a government which will look upon Canada not regionally but as a great nation among nations of this world.

While we were listening to these speeches I was reminded of the change of climate in this chamber over the space of a few years. While the group of which I sun a member for years has advocated the necessity for planning in freedom to provide a measure of basic security for all Canadians, members of other parties failed to agree with them. It is not so long ago that one of the members of the free enterprise parties in this house rose in his place and stated that any member of this house who suggests planning is suggesting reducing the Canadian people to slavery. I therefore think we must take some credit for creating a climate at least that is willing to consider this idea, if in some instances only in theory.
A perusal of the minister's speech and an examination of the bill very carefully in the time at my disposal causes me to say that in my opinion on this occasion the minister has blotted his McCutcheon.

speechtext:
The minister is such a kindly person that when speaking on the resolution preceding the bill he reminded me of the country doctor giving his patient a dose of soothing syrup and saying, "This may not cure you but it will make you feel a lot better". Without a doubt he is one of the most congenial and humane members of this house to man the ramparts of capitalism on this occasion.
I speak as a democratic socialist who believes that economic planning under the control of the parliament of Canada is the only alternative to the political dictatorship of communism and the growing economic dictatorship of monopoly capitalism. This afternoon there has been some reference to the question of freedom. The members of this group take this point of view with respect to the development of this economy because we believe in freedom. We do not believe that it should be the freedom of any Canadian to remain unemployed over a long period of months because his services are unrequired. The type of planning in which we believe is planning that places the responsibility for major policy in the hands of the people's representatives and not in the hands of the directors of a few corporations in Canada and not as now, should I say, in the majority of cases so far as large scale industry is concerned, in directorships held in New York and other large United States cities.


With all deference to the minister may I say that in my opinion this legislation is merely political window dressing. We will support it because it represents an idea. It shows we are making progress. They even accept the word "planning" now, even though they do not take action in that direction. I think it is a sop to the current interest in planning and the demand for planning in many quarters-a legislative wind, shall I say, to direct this current of thought into safe free enterprise planning.
When I criticize this legislation or any other legislation for members of our group, we do not do it with the thought that other people, because they believe other things are more appropriate, are unprincipled or immoral. We are simply placing on record our point of view in this house. Our points of view are largely determined as a result of our environment, our experience and our willingness to consider these problems as a result of reading, association, contacts with others and so on. In my few remarks which are always brief from my point of view, I will endeavour to prove my contentions by comments on the minister's speech, on the terms of the bill, on some of Senator McCutcheon's statements outside the house, and by reference given to this legislation by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) to the minister's remarks. I refer to his blessing on the principle of the bill. I am very glad he has returned to the chamber because I want to say a few complimentary things about him later.
I listened to the minister's speech very carefully and I thought it was very well put from his point of view. I also read it carefully. But I notice that this planning board will act in a very nebulous advisory capacity. There are no particular projects mentioned. There are no definitive suggestions as to the direction or approach that the board should take to our economic problems. There are no funds provided for any economic research in this direction or even research into projects rather than simply pure research into the mechanical aspects of economics. I do agree with the minister when he says that the aim is to provide a Canadian aspect to our development, rather than going in another direction; but after reading the terms of the bill I am afraid we will find that once again it is Canadian in name only, so far as major control of our economy is concerned.
I want to make a few comments on the bill and when the minister replies at the conclusion of the debate no doubt he will answer the questions I raise. We are very interested and have been for years in the proper development of our natural resources as the basis for the continued prosperity of

National Economic Development Board
this country and the maintenance of a reasonable and decent material standard of living. What we want to know is, does the bill anticipate planning with the provinces for the proper conservation and development of our natural resources? That is basic to the development of our whole economy. We realize that there are problems in this connection, but in our opinion it is the responsibility of both the federal and provincial governments to co-operate in planning the conservation, development and utilization of our natural resources. If we fail to do that in the near future, possibly we will have lost the opportunity for all time.
Does this bill provide for planning to return the ownership and control of foreign investment to Canadian governments and to Canadians generally? That is a question we want answered. Does the bill anticipate the establishment of a national development fund to promote public investment and does it anticipate the mobilization of private Canadian capital? In this connection I want to refer to the pipe line, not the debate in the house and the abuse of the rules of the house by the government of the day but the opportunity that was lost at that time because the government then did not believe in public ownership, in principle. The former Liberal government lent a large American corporation $86 million, I believe, to build a pipe line across Canada. That $86 million should have been public investment, and if it had been the investment would be paying a good return to the Canadian people at this time.
Does this bill anticipate legislation to correct the balance of payments problem? If we do not correct it within the next few years we will remain in financial servitude to the United States. The balance of payments problem arises primarily from foreign investments. Does the bill anticipate promotion by the government of Canadian participation in ownership and management of foreign owned industries? That is the first step that has to be taken by government. Does it anticipate the conversion of shares into bond issues so that we can look forward in the years to come to paying off this indebtedness, as was done in the United States, as was done in Sweden and as was also done in Norway years ago? Does this bill anticipate the type of planning that provides a system of taxation of dividends that will give the Canadian government control over the various aspects of the country's economic development?
Does this type of planning anticipate regulation to ensure operation of private enterprise to the advantage of Canadian consumers and workers generally? Does it anticipate regulation that will make foreign owned industries
conform to Canadian national policies with respect to export markets? That is something on which any government should take action in the very near future.
Does this bill anticipate the implementation of regulations that will prevent the hobbling of secondary industry by foreign owners? In that connection I should like to quote from the Globe and Mail of Tuesday, December 4, 1962. This situation is recognized even by persons who believe in the free enterprise system. The article from which I wish to quote is a dispatch from Ottawa under the heading, "Ottawa Viewpoint, Canadian Growth Lag Laid To Hobbling By Foreign Ownership", and reads in part as follows:
A professor of economics at Laval University, Roger Dehem, has looked back over the past five years of what he calls Canada's stunted growth-
One would not have thought that if one listened to the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny) last evening, but we all have different points of view.
-and offers an explanation for its cause-the hobbling of secondary industry by foreign owners.
The article continues, quoting the professor:
"I suggest that a basic factor inhibiting the growth of secondary manufacturing in Canada is not the smallness of the home market but the satellitic nature of most of our important firms," Professor Dehem asserted.
Then he goes on to say:
"The Canadian market has thus been glutted with high cost, high priced and often inferior American products. The inefficiency that is inherent in this structure seems to be a main cause of our stagnation in the past few years."
Professor Dehem charged that Canadian subsidiaries of foreign corporations are deliberately restricted to the domestic market rather than spreading out into world markets, and that high protection made them too inefficient to compete abroad.
No doubt this gentleman did not make this statement off the cuff. He has studied the question, and this is a problem that has got to be considered by those responsible to the government for a measure of report, shall I say, recommendation and so on with respect to planning.
I wish to make a few comments now with regard to the Minister without Portfolio whose name is Senator Wallace McCutcheon. I do so because, whatever happens with respect to the bill and whoever is chairman of the new board, we know that the grey eminence in the background will be this senator because he has been conscripted, I would almost say, to rescue the government from the economic morass into which it has sunk. I wish to quote from an article in Maclean's magazine
3000	HOUSE OF
National Economic Development Board of October 6, 1962 by Ken Lefolli headed, "Can These Men Run Canada Better?" It reads in part as follows:
"Whether the Prime Minister has realized it yet or not, Wally McCutcheon's threat to resign is all he needs to win an argument with anybody in the cabinet, including the Prime Minister himself."
These are the words of a man close to the cabinet who has worked with both McCutcheon and Nowlan. His opinion is the same one held by many other men in the upper ranks of government and business.
"John Diefenbaker has to satisfy Wally McCutcheon or wreck the Conservative party with every businessman in Canada, once and for all" the same man says. "McCutcheon is smart enough to know he's got the lever, and tough enough to pull it."
The article goes on to quote a caption in the Toronto Star of September 30, 1957 which reads: "Praises Canada's Drift Toward Welfare State." The account of a speech McCutcheon had made to the Canadian Club follows. Relating to the vast expansion of government and voluntary health and welfare programs, McCutcheon said:
You might expect me as a businessman to denounce this whole movement... as a dangerous, if not to say, pernicious thing. On the contrary, I regard it not only as one of the greatest achievements of private enterprise-
You know, the achievement is to rescue the casualties of capitalism and keep them alive in the meantime.
-and a modern industrial society, I consider it necessary to the continued existence of both.
Now, there are two different conceptions of social welfare. The one is that it is based on promoting the continued existence of the free enterprise system that makes the welfare society necessary because it props up the free enterprise system. E. P. Taylor has suggested another explanation that takes into account not only McCutcheon's good will-I am not questioning the hon. gentleman's good will. I am sure if a neighbour met him on the way from the parliament buildings to Wellington street and he was starving, the hon. gentleman would give him two bits.
E. P. Taylor has suggested, as I have said, another explanation that takes into account not only McCutcheon's good will, but the more conventional economic motive of selfinterest. Taylor is reported to have said, "What's good for Canada is good for Argus," when he was first asked to comment on McCutcheon's move, "and Wally McCutcheon is good for Canada". We cannot look into the future, and only the future can tell us whether or not that is true. Taylor's paraphrase of Charlie Wilson's statement, "What's good for General Motors is good for America", is less laughable than the original.
This afternoon one of our friends opposite in the Social Credit party made a very interesting speech. He showed the same concern


as other members of this house with our economic and social problems. He was complaining of the system. I give the hon. gentlemen credit. I am sure their hearts are in the right place, but they see us through a glass darkly. I am sure the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) will like that scriptural allusion. He was also complaining about the system. He really wants a form of planning, but he will not use the word. He substitutes the word "orientation". I think that is a good exercise in semantics. He used the word "orientation" when he wanted planning and would not use that word.
However, I thought the hon. gentleman's speech and the approach by the sponsors of this bill clearly indicated that the planning they envisage will be very different from the planning we consider necessary to provide permanent economic stability for Canada. We do not overlook the difficulty. We are not suggesting there is some complete, overnight solution. We are suggesting a change of direction with regard to our approach to these questions.
Last evening, I listened to the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny) with great interest. He talked about the prosperity that this government had brought to Canada. We find that in 1962 the profits of the major companies in Canada were considerably increased. I am not going to take the time of the house to deal with the figures. Possibly some other member of this group will. Profits were considerably increased. While Canada and Canadians generally are suffering certain economic disadvantages, and while small businessmen and workers are unemployed, including farmers and others, the profit ratio rose. At the same time we have something over 400,000 people unemployed at the present time.
At the same time, the minister said we have got to find ways and means of increasing production. They will not find a solution to this question until they accept their responsibilities as representatives of the people of Canada in this connection. I should like to make another reference to this question of planning and the approach of those who are now using the word. In the Gazette of December 11, 1962, there is a report of a speech by R. A. Emerson, vice president of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The article reads in part:
Master plan for economy Is opposed.
C.P.R. Vice President R. A. Emerson of Montreal said Monday Canada needs to plan for the future but must avoid at all costs having its economic life ordered and predetermined according to a master plan.
He said:
I have interpreted the remarks of the Minister of Finance in the house to mean that the national

economic development board is intended to provide an advisory service and, more particularly, to look ahead, to detect the trend of things to come and to recommend policies for government to assist in achieving economic development.
The article reads:
Mr. Emerson said a planned economy must interfere with the normal functions of the market place.
What he means is, interfere with the normal decisions of the large corporations of this country. I think these remarks by this gentleman indicate that their approach to planning and the approach of this government to planning is opposed to ours. It is the same attitude as we have had towards planning in every direction. They are willing to have a measure of planning, provided there is no interference with the vested interests in this country.
I want to refer for a moment or two to the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and to his support for the principle of the bill. I always listen with interest to the hon. member for Essex East when he speaks with his organ-like tone. He gave his blessing to the principle of the bill, singing seven-fold amens to the minister's statement on the principle. You know, he is an impressive speaker, the hon. member for Essex East. I remember a few sessions ago sitting in the house when the minister spoke for some 40 minutes. I walked out to the front entrance, and a gentleman from Texas went to the front door just as there was a clergyman coming in. The Texan went up to this clergyman and said, "Sir, can you tell me the name of this cathedral"? This illustrates that the hon. member for Essex East is such an impressive speaker he causes people to believe they are in a cathedral.
Why did this hon. member endorse the principle of the bill and then later on make some qualifying comments? The reason is that the party on the government side of the house and the party on the opposite side of the house, the Liberal party, both believe in the free enterprise system as practised to date. However, there are a lot of humane members amongst these parties and they are quite willing to spend a bit of money to rescue the casualties of this system. Now, those who feel that the progressive Liberals worship on the altar of free enterprise propped up by the welfare state-
