Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Finance spoke on this bill on November 27 last he expressed its purpose as follows, as reported at page 2073 of Hansard:
The government is determined that this country will continue to prosper and to grow. It is determined to stimulate the further expansion of our existing industries and to encourage even further the development in Canada of new and efficient industries.
Surely if these admirable objectives, with which all of the hon. members of this house can agree, were attained, we would, although the minister did not quite say so, have a country blessed by full employment. But what we must ask ourselves here and what the people of Canada have a right to know is whether the passage of this bill and its implementation will achieve this admirable aim. The debate to date, I submit, has not been too hopeful. It has concerned itself almost exclusively with the hope that the planning proposed will help to develop new industry. The development of new industry is important but it is only one side of the coin. The rapid relocation of existing manufacturing and servicing industries from old established centres towards a concentration in a few major areas in Canada is having a growing and disastrous effect on the Canadian people. Decisions by management as to plant location have, to the detriment of Canada, been regarded by private industry and by governments, both Liberal and Conservative, as the concern of business alone, despite the fact that the welfare of

National Economic Development Board
entire communities and the lives of thousands of our citizens are affected by the movement of plants and factories. Surely it is time that the desire for profit and competitive advantage which industry hopes to gain when it moves to new locations should be considered and balanced against the responsibility of those same industries to the communities in which they were for so long established.
Unfortunately, if we look at corporation examples or at the view of either the present government or the official opposition when they were in power, and when we see how they discuss this bill, it is obvious that to them profit is still the overriding if not the only motive for every act carried out by the corporations of Canada. This government has no intention of even trying to blunt this unconscionable drive for profit at any cost by Canadian business.
Corporate decisions on plant location have had for the people of Canada and our economy consequences many times greater than any decision of democratically elected governments, whether federal, provincial or municipal. In this bill or in the speeches which have been made in this house by representatives of the government or of the official opposition explaining their position, there is nothing to indicate that the situation will be better in the near future if they have their way.
Governments have looked with indifference at the haphazard growth and development of our economy because of the unregulated concentration of industry and population. Without real planning and the desire to meet specific problems there will be and there is no end in sight to the decline of employment in many of our major towns and cities. Canada will increasingly become the scene of many depressed and underdeveloped areas surrounding two islands of concentrated prosperity, namely Montreal in one province and Toronto-Hamilton in Ontario.
The government has made it clear that this bill is proposing another advisory board like the productivity council, the Atlantic development board and a host of others that are being established. This board will have no more power to get action than those already working have had. The productivity council sent a mission to western Europe. It was made up of representatives of labour, management and government. It made an excellent report, which members of this house have had an opportunity to read, on western Europe's prosperity and how it has been accomplished. What minister or what government department has the responsibility to see that we apply to Canada those lessons which they
learned, so that we can do for the people of Canada the kind of job which the western European countries have been able to do for the last 15 years. This is completely unlike the European experience. We can only assume from these differences between what is being done in Europe and what is proposed in this bill that the bill is really nothing but window dressing and will accomplish nothing to bring us to the state of full employment which they are enjoying in Europe.
In most European countries they have dealt directly with the problem of plant location through area development programs. In Great Britain positive controls and financial inducements are used to direct the location of new plants. A company wishing to build a new plant may be refused permission to locate in an area where there is a labour shortage. At the same time, loans, grants and other inducements are offered to encourage the location of plants in areas of higher than average unemployment. Thousands of new jobs have been created in formerly depressed areas by these policies. The president of the British board of trade used his power of persuasion in not permitting the Ford Motor Company of Great Britain to expand its own original location in London, which is already congested, and persuaded the company to erect its new facilities on the Mersey side, an area suffering from chronic and high unemployment. Twenty thousand new jobs were created in this area. Is it too much to suggest that we could use some of the same type of persuasion and direction in Canada?
What has happened in Canada, of course, is the exact reverse. Beginning in 1957 when the former government was still in power and continuing until the present day we have had a steady erosion of jobs in the Windsor area as the automobile industry has moved its facilities to the Toronto-Hamilton area. But you can study this bill or the speeches of the minister with a microscope and find no evidence that this government proposes to do anything like the British have accomplished.
In France recently the French minister of industry threatened, under the power vested in him by French law, to examine with the greatest care new foreign investment in France because two American firms had laid off 1,000 workers as a result of changed business conditions. The Toronto Globe and Mail in its issue of Friday, December 14, 1962, quoted the minister as follows:
I will not permit that certain isolated enterprises practice in French industry an irresponsible policy
3016	HOUSE OF
National Economic Development Board that does not respect the social contract linking a financially powerful enterprise to the labour it employs.
That is a far cry from anything we have heard from any minister in this house. The French government, on the advice of the commissariat du plan, prohibits new installations in the Paris area, and there are grants and fiscal exemptions to encourage development in certain other regions. If it were not so tragic in its consequences it would be laughable that a United States foreign subsidiary 3,000 miles across the Atlantic ocean from its parent head office is subject to this kind of social restraint when in Canada in the Windsor area, only a few miles away from its parent company, another huge subsidiary company in the same industry is absolutely free and unchecked by any such moral or legal restraint in this country. Yet we have this happening with no protest on the part of the government and no protest at the time it began by the former government which is now the official opposition.
There is not a single industrialized society in free enterprise western Europe which does not, in some form or another curb the power of huge corporations to disregard their social and moral responsibilities not only to the individual worker in their employ but to the national interest as a whole. How different it is in Canada in the year 1963. We continue to propose more incentives to industry when the problem is not only to attract new industries but rather to retain established industries in the communities in which they have been established for many years and to which, I suggest, they have a real responsibility.
Our programs, existing and proposed, are programs which can only be described as piecemeal and which will have little effect on the people of this country. In Europe they realize that particular areas require special attention in order that they can contribute fully to the over-all economic growth of the country as a whole. The European programs concern themselves with much more than the elimination of pockets of high unemployment and the rehabilitation of distressed areas. They make plans for the country as a whole.
One of the best examples of the lack of planning and the callousness of Canadian industry can be seen if one looks at the city of Windsor. The exodus of industry there has means the loss of thousands of jobs. Many of the unemployed have never found new employment. Since 1956, when the Liberal party was still the government of Canada, there has been a drastic contraction of employment in Windsor. There has been a drop of $20 million a year in wages and salaries alone. As income from wages and salaries fell so
IMr. Orlikow.]

has income earned by business, professional and commercial interests in that area. New residential construction has fallen off sharply in the past five years. In 1961 house building was one third of that of 1956. Per capita spending on retail goods and services declined by $20 between 1959 and 1961.
Greater Windsor's population increased by only 18 per cent from 1951 to 1961, while the average increase for 17 metropolitan areas surveyed for the same period was 45 per cent. From 1956 to 1961 the increase in population in Windsor was only 4 per cent.
The major cause for this stagnation in Windsor is the program of relocation of Windsor's single major industry, the motor vehicle and parts industry. There has been no compensating growth in other lines of manufacturing so Windsor is plagued by large scale chronic unemployment. In 1951 the Ford Motor Company of Canada had 12,000 production workers in Windsor. Today there are less than 4,000, and more departments are to be transferred to the Toronto area in the next few years.
This fantastic cut-back was part of a deliberate policy on the part of the company to diversify and make more competitive the domestic manufacturing plants of Ford of Canada. The company has withdrawn from Windsor with little, if any, consideration for its displaced workers. Supply and feeder plants which sell to Ford have been forced to follow Ford to the Toronto-Oakville area. There are now more of these plants in the Toronto area than are left in the greater Windsor area. Thousands of these workers laid off by Ford and the parts plants have never been re-employed and are now drawing unemployment insurance benefits or, in many cases, welfare from the municipalities concerned because they have exhausted their benefits.
Many attempts were made to get the company to consider the effects of these moves or even to help the workers move to the new location so that they could start over with a new job in a new area, but these attempts were met with cold, hard, ruthless, callous disregard by the companies concerned and especially by the Ford company. This is not a case of a company being forced to take drastic action by adversity. For the first six months of 1962 the Ford Motor Company showed a consolidated net income of over $20 million, an increase of 145 per cent over the same period in 1961. The net profit for the first six months of 1962 was almost $5 million higher than its previous record. From 1951 to 1961 the earnings retained by Ford for use in the business rose from $178 million to $226 million. In the ten year period ended in 1960 the net profit of Ford represented an average

annual return of over 11 per cent on the company's average net worth for that period. Certainly this was a generous rate of return. Yet despite this generous rate of return the Ford workers and the community of Windsor have been ignored and their welfare disregarded by this corporate giant, a giant without a heart. Ford can reap record profits, but it cannot or will not find the means to provide employment for workers who have worked for that company for 20 or more years. This company is one of the wealthiest in Canada. The people of Canada, I suggest, have a right to ask how profitable a company has to be before it realizes that it has a responsibility to its workers, to the people of Canada as well as to its shareholders.
If this bill has any answer for the workers of Windsor, I for one have failed to find it. The private corporations, however, are not the only ones who are guilty of a callous disregard of their own workers. In my own city of Winnipeg, we have seen the gradual movement of the T.C.A. operations to Montreal. Trans-Canada Air Lines head office was originally in Winnipeg. In recent years a large number of departments of T.C.A. have been moved east. Included amongst these are the headquarters and staff, engineering, communications laboratory, radio shop, instrument shop, materials and processing laboratory and the engine overhaul shop.
In 1948, Mr. C. D. Howe, then Minister of Trade and Commerce, said that there was no intention to move T.C.A.'s main department from Winnipeg. He said that 95 per cent of the activities at Winnipeg would remain there. In December, 1948, Mr. Gordon McGregor, then president of T.C.A., replying to rumours that T.C.A. contemplated moving its overhaul base to Montreal, said that some of the executive staff might be moved to Montreal but that the company had no intention of transferring the overhaul base. In February, 1949, Mr. McGregor announced that administrative offices of the operations department of T.C.A. would move to Montreal the next fall. He said:
There is no conceivable reason nor any grounds for suspicion that this move marks the beginning of a mass transfer of T.C.A. activities to Montreal.
In November, 1949, Mr. Howe said that T.C.A. did not contemplate making further transfer of personnel from Winnipeg to other centres. In October, 1951, a T.C.A. official said that the Winnipeg overhaul base has been, is and will continue to be the system's only complete repair base. In November 1951, Mr. McGregor said Winnipeg would share in the steady development of T.C.A. all across the country. In February, 1956, T.C.A. officials 27507-3-191
National Economic Development Board announced that T.C.A. was dropping major overhaul work in aircraft radio equipment in Winnipeg.
In September, 1957, T.C.A. officials emphatically denied rumours that the overhaul and maintenance base was being moved from Winnipeg. In 1957, November, Mr. George Hees, then minister of transport, said T.C.A. employees in Winnipeg had no need to fear for their future employment because T.C.A. did not expect in any way to diminish repair and maintenance operations in Winnipeg. In January, 1959, Mr. McGregor said that T.C.A. had no plans to decimate its shop staff in Winnipeg. In January, 1961, it was reported that a letter from Mr. Hees to the Manitoba government said that T.C.A.'s overhaul base in Winnipeg might be closed in 1965 or shortly thereafter.
In 1961, May, the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) told the St. James chamber of commerce that T.C.A. was reducing the volume of its overhaul work in Winnipeg but that the overhaul of Viscounts would continue in Winnipeg at least through 1965. Most of the groups which I have listed have since increased greatly in scope and numbers of personnel. The total staff of T.C.A. has increased sharply, all the increases of course being in eastern Canada. Now, plans are being completed to consolidate all overhaul facilities in Montreal. The transport minister has suggested that this can be done, and I quote, "Without major disruption to the lives of employees or the economic welfare of Winnipeg."
What nonsense this is, to imply that over 1,500 employees with a payroll of almost a million dollars a month can be uprooted from their homes and families in Winnipeg without major disruption to their lives or to the city of Winnipeg. This is, at best, a dream of the minister's which will be a nightmare for the people of Winnipeg. Hundreds of employees will not or could not move. They have homes, they have families, they have responsibilities in Winnipeg. There is little, if any, alternative employment for this highly skilled group in Winnipeg. By one decision of T.C.A. management, more jobs will be lost in Winnipeg by 1966 than the whole aggressive industry searching program of the Manitoba government, for which they recently received an international award, could possibly find.
Not only will this decision mean a payroll loss to Winnipeg of almost $1 million a month, with consequent loss of purchasing power for goods and services of about $14 million a year, but it will mean the loss of a valuable place of employment for the skilled workers now being trained in our technical
3018	HOUSE OF
National Economic Development Board and vocational schools. It will depress the housing market when close to 1200 homeowners have to move, and it will certainly disrupt homes and families. Why is this move being promoted? It is supposedly being promoted because of economic necessity, but the report has never been made public. It has been rumoured that the savings to be made are in the nature of $1 million a year. Even if this is true, this is a relatively small amount when compared to the social and economic loss of the whole prairie region. It is a pretty poor choice that is being made.
T.C.A.'s behaviour is puzzling because it is supposed to be a publicly owned company whose main purpose is service, not profit. But this government, and the Liberal government that preceded it, have harangued T.C.A. and other crown corporations into acting like private concerns in order to show a good balance sheet, regardless of the social consequences involved. Yet the government, which promises planning every time it introduces this type of legislation which we are now discussing, permits this callous disregard of human need while preaching the virtues of planning. The type of planning envisioned by this government may prove to be worth less than nothing but it will raise the hopes of the Canadian people without really accomplishing anything.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, it is time for Canada to stop treating unemployment as if it were an incurable disease. It is time we realized that some parts of Canada, the maritimes, the prairies, parts of Quebec and parts of Ontario, like Windsor, are being underdeveloped and are falling into decline, while other parts of Canada are being overdeveloped. Every day we hear of plants moving to these favourite areas. We see housing and community facilities in other areas abandoned, while they are duplicated in the select few cities which are growing. This represents a tremendous waste of resources.
We need a new approach in this country if we are to improve our dismal record of inadequate economic growth and the resultant huge and persistent unemployment. This new approach calls for the adoption of real economic planning at both the federal and provincial levels. Only such planning can achieve the goal we should all be striving for, full employment and full production. Unfortunately, nothing which has been said by either the government representatives or the opposition to date would indicate that they have really learned anything from the difficulties in Canada or the successes in other countries, so that we can hope or expect to achieve the goals of full production or full employment from the measures which they have or are likely to propose.

I expected that obvious retort. I will tell the junior minister of citizenship and immigration that in this particular case his knowledge is not as complete as he suggests.
Now, Mr. Chairman, having in mind the announcement made by the Minister of Finance on the resolution stage, every member of this committee had a right to assume we were going to receive from the government a proposal of the most fundamental character. I do not think I understate the feelings of members on the government side or in the opposition, nor do I think I misrepresent the feeling in the country generally, When I say there is great disappointment that this much touted measure should be as weak as a perusal of the bill clearly confirms it to be.
We were told by the minister that at long last the government, because of the existence of certain serious problems facing this nation, including our balance of payments problem, our trading relations problems and others, had decided there had to be a new technique in the Canadian pattern of administration to make the ordering of our affairs more efficient to meet the difficulties which face us at this time. We were reminded by the minister of the work which has been undertaken in France and in some other European countries. We were told by some hon. members of the recommendations which had been made by the special mission of the productivity council to Europe, and, because of those initial observations by the Minister of Finance, we all thought we were going to be presented with a new instrument in the government of our country, an instrument which would make the administration of our affairs more efficient to deal with the serious economic problems which face us. Thus, there is great disappointment, on examination of this bill, to find that it lacks even some of the stronger provisions which were to be found in the Atlantic development board measure.
What have we got? We have now a series of boards in being and others are being brought into being by this government. We have the Atlantic development board, and we all know the deficiencies of that particular instrument. We are going to have the advisory council on industrial change and manpower adjustment to be introduced later by the Minister of Labour. We have the national productivity council and now we have this economic development board. This is the board of which the Prime Minister spoke at the Chateau Laurier at the end of last week, indicating that this was the heart and the core of the long term program of this government which,
he said, is prepared to face dynamically and with vigour the problems which confront the country at the present time.
Let us now examine the consequences of this proliferation of boards, referred to by the hon. member for York South the other day in his speech, when he discussed this particular proposal. As he said, when hon. members opposite dealt with the suggestion which we made in 1959, hon. gentlemen said that we would have too many boards. And now they themselves, as a result of the Atlantic development board, the national productivity council, the advisory council on industrial change and manpower adjustment, and now this economic development board, are guilty of the very proliferation which they themselves accused us of promoting when we suggested the establishment of a national economic advisory council in 1959.
There is, moreover, no co-ordination whatsoever between the various bodies. We have problems, which the Prime Minister recognized a week after the election as being of an emergent character, now to be tackled by four distinct boards, all having in fact the same purpose, all four operating under a different minister. Is it any wonder then that we recognize in the measure now before the house one that is incapable of meeting the current national situation, as a new instrument of government to supplement the activities of the government itself in seeking to cope with the various problems which face the country?
It is significant that the Minister of Finance, when he proposed this measure, not once used the word "planning". We have a right to ask the minister, as we shall when we come to discuss the clauses of the bill, whether this was an intentional omission. It is true that the minister for northern affairs used the word planning. It is true that several individual private members sitting behind the Minister of Finance used the word planning. But not the Minister of Finance. We have a right to ask the Minister of Finance, was this done by design? Because if this is the case, then we must observe that the minister does not agree with the unanimous recommendations which were made to the productivity council by the special mission to Europe of that council, recommendations which I think represent one of the most important and significant contributions made by any Canadian body appointed by the federal government for a very long time. If the minister does not want to use the word "planning" because he does not believe in it, then let him say so. If he does take that position, then we will have to recognize that this bill does nothing more than add another instrument to the Department of Finance, giving to the Department of Finance and its
3022	HOUSE OF
National Economic Development Board minister another official or series of officials to assist him in the operation and administration of that particular department.
That is not what the minister said this bill was going to do. This was a bill which was going to enable the government as a whole-not only the Department of Finance but the government as a whole-to give greater preparatory consideration to problems such as unemployment, the relocation of industry-a corollary of that problem-our balance of payments position, our trading relation problems, our fiscal and tax problems, and the proper equation of the responsibilities between the two senior levels of government. In other words, we were going to have a bill which would do for Canada what was being done by a similar measure in France and by a similar measure in the United Kingdom.
That is not what is now before us in Bill No. C-87. There is nothing in this bill that compares with the kind of organization, for instance, that they have in France. The hon. member for York South yesterday said that we on this side of the house had talked about the system of planning in France and about the kind of national development board which had been set up in that country, but that no one but he himself really seemed to have any understanding about what they were doing in France. Well, there will be ample opportunity during the course of our discussions to ascertain precisely what we understand to be the role of the national economic development board in France, although that is not the title of that body. We will want to know whether or not the government believes in the principle underlying that particular operation in France; whether the government has in mind anything like "Neddy", the national economic development organization in the United Kingdom, the chairman of which, incidentally, happens to be the chancellor of the exchequer. We will want to know whether or not the government believes in any kind of planning. We have not advocated in this Liberal opposition planned economy, but we have said that in the light of the character of problems of the modern day economic society in Canada there has to be some kind of planning. It is not the kind of planning suggested by the socialists. It is the kind of planning which the major countries in western Europe have embarked upon with great success, to meet their economic problems. Is the government in favour of indicative planning as they have in France? Or is it in favour of the kind of planning technique of Western Germany? Are they in favour of the kind of planning which they have in Sweden? Are we entitled to have answers from the minister to these precise
[Mr. Martin (Essex East).)

questions? Otherwise we will conclude that this bill is nothing but a facade, nothing but an attempt to deceive the Canadian people once again into believing that this government has taken strong action to meet these problems which face the country.
This will not be the first time that we have had bills presented by this government to the house which look good in form, which make a great public appeal, but which on analysis have been shown to be absolutely worthless and ineffective to do the job for which allegedly they are designed. How is this bill going to help, for instance, in the problem of relocating industry? A few moments ago the hon. member for Winnipeg North spoke of economic conditions in the city from which I come, of the decision of certain corporations in that community to locate elsewhere with the consequence that there have been large numbers of men and women placed in the category of unemployed persons. What is this bill going to do about this kind of problem? It will be no answer to say that this is largely a provincial problem. It will be no answer to say that this is a problem which resides with another jurisdiction. It is true that under the property and civil rights clause of our constitution the provinces alone can take action along certain lines not open to this government. But if this national economic development board is going to mean anything, it must mean that the government in this instrument is setting up a body that will be capable of working out with the provinces arrangements to meet the particular problem of unemployment which exists in certain areas such as the one from which I come and, in certain areas in the Atlantic provinces, referred to a few moments ago by the hon. member for Essex West.
What is this bill going to do about the problem of unemployment? The Minister of Finance cannot say to us, "This is not the problem of the Department of Finance; address your question to the Minister of Labour". If this bill does not set up the facility by which the government will have some supplementary assistance in providing an answer to unemployment, then it is practically worthless.
We now have a serious problem of unemployment in our country with 73,000 more people unemployed in the last reported month than in the previous one. We have close to 500,000 people out of work. It is the job of this government to find ways and means, in co-operation with labour and management to provide an answer to this problem. It is the job of a board like this one to assist in resolving the kind of situation which has resulted from our balance of payments

National Economic Development Board
problem. Yet, if we look at the objects and the powers of the board we shall find that no effort is going to be made by this board to deal with problems of this character. Hence we are warranted to say that, while this bill is good in principle in that it creates the necessary framework for doing something worth while, we must say that, as it is at present, particularly in sections 9, 12 and 22, it is not capable of justifying the assertions made by the Minister of Finance with regard to its merits.
We are not told anything by the minister in this bill about what the relations between the Atlantic development board will be; what the relations between the Atlantic development board and the advisory council will be; what the relations between this economic development board and the national productivity council will be. Oh, I know we are told in the bill that there will be cooperation between this particular national economic development board and the other boards. However, we are not told how that co-operation will be effected. This board is treated as an equal of the national productivity council and of the Atlantic development board.
No one denies that the Atlantic development board is designed to meet an important area problem. We all recognize that fact and we said so when that bill was discussed, although we thought the bill was not capable of meeting the objectives which the Minister of National Revenue projected for that measure when he presented it to this House of Commons shortly before Christmas. But surely the problems facing the people in the Atlantic provinces, apart from their special severity and intensity, are not unlike the problems which face most areas of Canada at the present time. The basic problems of the Atlantic provinces are the basic problems of Canada. This national economic development board bill ought to take into account this elementary fact but this is something which it does not do.
Surely the minister cannot be allowed to pass over the extremely important report to which I have already referred, namely the report of the labour-management-government mission to Europe to the national productivity council. This is a monumental document. It represents the considered opinion of important segments of our country. I refer to management, labour, capital, government, agriculture, the universities and other important segments of Canadian thinking. On this special mission there were important men representing large corporations. They included men such as the president of the Goodrich Rubber Company, and
important officials of the Canadian Labour Congress. The members of this commission were unanimous in the recommendations they made to the government.
On examination of this report hon. members will find that these men have made a careful analysis of what is done through national development boards in Sweden, the Netherlands, West Germany, France, Belgium and England, where they have resorted in varying measure to the principle of economic planning to meet the problem of unemployment and other problems, many of which we have in even greater intensity in this country at the present time. This report has concluded that the gap between labour-government-management co-operation in Canada as compared with the situation in Europe is so serious as as to warrant the conclusion that many of our problems in this country at this time arise from the fact that we have not established between labour and management under government sponsorship the confidence necessary to increase productivity so as to put us in a competitive position with other countries, with the consequence of having a salutary effect on the level of employment in our country.
Can we fully discuss this bill without having from the Minister of Finance a careful assessment of how the government looks upon this measure? Are we not entitled to ask the Minister of Finance whether or not, as the result of the passing of the national economic development board bill, the government is going to take vigorous steps at once to implement the recommendations of this particular special mission of able and representative people in our country who have come to these unanimous conclusions?
It will be no answer for the Minister of Finance to say that this is a report made to the productivity council and not a report made to the national economic development board, and that consequently we must await a discussion of the amendment to the National Productivity Council Act before receiving from the government its final appreciation of the recommendations contained in this report of this special mission to Europe of the labour-management committee of the national productivity council. If that is the reply of the minister, then we shall have had a clear indication of the meaningless intentions which the government really has in mind with regard to the implementation of Bill No. C-87, an act to provide for the establishment of a national economic development board.
The real fact is that the purposes of the national productivity council and of the Atlantic development board and of the advisory
3024	HOUSE OF COMMONS
National Economic Development Board council on industrial change and manpower adjustment are the same as the reasons which warrant our giving consideration to the setting up of a national economic development board, such as that which in principle is proposed in this bill. Is it a fact that, as a result of the co-operation between labour and management in France, it has been possible to place corporate enterprise in that country in a competitive position with other countries in Europe and elsewhere in the world? Is it true that as a result of the relationship between the farming community and government and other segments of opinion that it has been possible for West Germany to enjoy the improved economic standards which have come to that portion of divided Germany? Is it because of the establishment of "Neddy" in the United Kingdom that many of the problems of that country have been in large measure, if not fully, resolved and settled in a manner that has enabled that country to be picked out as an example of what we might do, for instance, in the matter of the relocation of industry?
Is it going to be possible under this bill for recommendations to be made to the Minister of Finance, for blueprints to be given, which will clearly establish the procedure by which it will be possible for the national government in co-operation with the provinces to take cognizance of the considerations that are now encompassed, for instance, by the town and country act in the United Kingdom and the unemployment act of the United Kingdom of 1960?
These are questions with regard to which we have a right at this stage of the proceedings on this bill to ask the minister for definite responses in order to assess the value of this measure. We believed, as we stated in this house shortly after the present government came into office, when we were confronted with high levels of unemployment and when there was every indication from all the indices that we were going to have unemployment over a period of years, that the best way to tackle this problem was to establish a national economic development body, made up of representatives of the various occupational sections of our country to enable the government to have a comprehensive view of the situation and to formulate plans by which the government could apply itself vigorously to problems which cried for solution then, and which have gone unresolved since that time. That is not what we have here today. I say to the Minister of Finance, that from the statement he made in the house before adjournment I cannot conceive that he has given any evidence that the government proposes to use this bill to resort to
[Mr. Martin (Essex East).!
extraordinary action to meet an extraordinary situation in our country. I say to him that anything short of such action will not satisfy the Canadian people and will not satisfy this house.
We have discussed unemployment in this house for a number of years, since the government came into office. This is the first time that the government has come forward with a measure which in principle is capable of providing the machinery to cope with unemployment. If given the necessary power, if given the necessary consensus, if given the necessary sponsorship, this bill could do something to meet the serious problems facing us, some of which I have mentioned in a general way. But I say to the minister that there is nothing in the bill to warrant the conclusion that this is the intention and purpose that the government has in mind in the bill it has brought forward.
We shall offer amendments to the bill. We will deal with it clause by clause and we will offer our comments and our amendments which, if adopted, we believe will give the bill the character it should have and which we thought it was going to have, when the minister referred to the bill as a revolutionary measure. If this represents the minister's understanding of the word "revolutionary", I can only say that we never need fear that there will be any kind of ordinary change in this country as long as the minister is in a position to influence the character of the Canadian revolution.
A careful reading of the bill reveals clearly that it is merely a gesture. It is a facade. It is a concession to modern times begrudgingly given rather than an attempt to forge a new instrument of national development, which is what we thought the bill was going to be. That is what the Prime Minister said the bill was going to be when he spoke to the Conservative convention last week. I am sure that the Prime Minister, occupied as he is now with many questions, has not had time to read the bill or he would never have made the statement he made last Friday when speaking to the members of his party.
Today we recognize the interdependence of all sectors of our economy. We know that the farmer cannot prosper while the automobile worker goes without wages. Dislocation of one sector is rapidly transmitted with serious repercussions to another. It is no longer feasible to plan in isolation.
What then should be the aim of this legislation? I say in reply, the creation of an institutional framework for a new economic consensus, a joint seeking of ways of attaining agreed levels of national development. Nothing less than this will satisfy the Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, if we consider the events of the last five years, we realize that for the Conservative party, economic development has meant deficit after deficit and also the growing problem of unemployment, which has increased steadily.
On the other hand, if we consider the last 22 years of Liberal administration, we realize that to them economic development meant an increase in taxes, with a view to developing high finance and chartered banks, as it can be seen today.
That is why, after 22 years of taxes under a Liberal government, I was not too much impressed by the very eloquent speech of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) who preceded me; it was a forceful speech, that is all. But unfortunately, he only plays second fiddle in his party. If he had been selected as leader, then I would have believed that the Liberal party would have done what he stated earlier.
But since he plays only second fiddle and the first violin changes tune quite often, Mr. Chairman, I refuse to rely in any way on what those tail-riding individuals have to say, because the leader and the fellow sitting on his left, representing the chartered banks have always been the ones who called the tune in that party.
Mr. Chairman. I have been listening to Liberal speeches for many years in the province of Quebec, and I have always thought that they were great talkers, but were actually accomplishing very little. In a word, little action is the motto of the Liberal party.
I sometimes hear that the bill should attempt to balance our international payments. Now, we realize that the imbalance started following the war and gradually developed until it reached its present situation.
This year, we are facing a balance of payments deficit of about $770 million arising 27507-3-192
mostly from the payment to foreigners, of interest and dividends out of our industries and our Canadian capital.
Mr. Chairman, I should like, in the light of the bill now before us, to develop especially this principle. It is very easy to expand our economy should we want to do so. Our natural resources are looked upon with envy by all the other countries. But, to my way of thinking, the great difficulty in the past was that we have not developed our economy by Canadians and for Canadians.
This is the purpose which must be achieved. I believe, and I am quite satisfied that hon. members in this house will want to agree with us that there might be reasons why we, French Canadians, realize more than English speaking Canadians that our economy is controlled by foreigners and that the profits are also going abroad.
If a French Canadian, wandering on one of the main streets of the metropolis of Toronto, sees an English Canadian name on the door of a firm, he is inclined to wonder who is really the owner of that company. The English Canadian, noticing the same name, automatically believes that this industry is controlled by Canadians.
When we see the name Aluminum Company of Canada on the walls of a building, we wonder who are the owners of this company. But when the English Canadian sees the same name on the same building, it is reasonable to expect that he will not have the same doubts as to the ownership of this company. It should be stated that the Aluminum Company of Canada is owned by the Mellon Bank in the United States.
When I see an English name on a building, I make inquiries about it, but an English speaking person is inclined to believe that the company is managed by Canadians because the name is English.
Mr. Chairman, my point is that foreigners, unfortunately, have too much control over our economy at the present time. As much as 75 and even 80 per cent of our economy is believed to be under foreign control.
Hence, we, citizens of a free country, who want to be free citizens, realize that, after all, we are but an economic colony of a foreign country.
Mr. Chairman, two great races make up the population of our country, Canada. They have always been proud of their freedom, of owning their country and of developing it for their own benefit.
In fact, I have never heard it said-and history has never proved it-that Englishmen, in England, would not have shed their last

National Economic Development Board drop of blood to protect the natural resources and the industry of their country. They own their country, just as the French do in France.
They make it a point of honour to develop their industry, to control their trade and their factories.
Should we believe that when those two races crossed the ocean to settle in Canada, that their blood became so much thinner that we, the descendants of those two great English and French races, should accept today, without moving, without protesting in any way, to be dominated as we are by foreign industrialists, no matter to what country they belong? Are we going to allow our natural resources, our industries and our manufactures to be in the hands, not of Canadian citizens, but of foreign companies, whatever country they may come from?
Mr. Chairman, I think it is time to bring this situation to the attention of Canadian citizens, to my fellow English speaking as well as French speaking citizens.
Some English speaking citizens criticized our educational system. They stated facts. But I think it is time that in this house, we should state some facts to our English speaking Canadian citizens so that they will realize that just like us, they must free themselves from foreign control or domination of our industries, our natural resources, our trade and in short, our country's economy.
English speaking citizens must face the situation. That situation should raise reactions among them, it should be a spur that will make them work with us so that we may become masters of our own economy, and so that when we produce and make profits every year, those profits do not always go to foreign countries like they did this year, for instance, when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) complained of a deficit of $770 million.
Speaking of that deficit, the minister said it was not a deficit resulting from the sale of goods, but a deficit caused by the fact that we must pay interest and profits to foreign countries on the development of our industry.

Canada is losing $770 million a year simply because citizens of other countries have been granted the right to come and develop our natural resources.
Mr. Chairman, I think we have there a situation which should be seriously considered by every Canadian citizen. We should try to find the means to free ourselves from this foreign control over our economy, in order to develop our country to our own advantage.
Mr. Chairman, when we realize that not only our money but also our natural resources are going to foreign countries, we cannot but come to the conclusion that there is something abnormal in this case.
